blocks.text: A urine dipstick is a rapid, semi-quantitative diagnostic test used to detect chemical abnormalities in urine. It is commonly examined in medicine, pediatrics, obstetrics and gynecology, emergency medicine and primary care OSCEs.

The examiner may ask you to identify the strip, explain what it detects, demonstrate correct testing, interpret a colour chart, identify sources of error and explain when further investigations are necessary.
Name: Urine reagent strip, urinalysis dipstick or urine dipstick.
Classification: Point-of-care chemical diagnostic test.
Distinguishing features:
A narrow plastic strip with multiple chemically impregnated reagent pads.
Each pad changes colour when exposed to particular substances or chemical conditions in urine.
Results are interpreted using the manufacturer's colour chart or a compatible automated reader.
Different products contain different combinations of test pads.
Tests several parameters simultaneously, often including pH, protein, glucose, blood, ketones, nitrite, leukocyte esterase, specific gravity, bilirubin and urobilinogen.
Designed for a particular analyte or screening purpose, such as protein or glucose, depending on the product.
A reagent strip read by an automated or semi-automated analyser to improve consistency of timing and colour interpretation.
OSCE identification statement:

“This is a urine reagent dipstick, a point-of-care diagnostic strip used to detect and estimate the concentration of selected chemical constituents in urine. It is commonly used to screen for urinary abnormalities, including proteinuria, glycosuria, haematuria and findings that may support a diagnosis of urinary tract infection.”

rows: Ketones, with blood glucose and blood ketones assessed as indicated
Urinary protein when clinically indicated; the dipstick does not establish pregnancy
Protein screening, followed by quantitative assessment when indicated
Specific gravity as one component of assessment
Selected chemical abnormalities as part of the clinical evaluation

blocks.text: Important limitations:
A urine dipstick does not definitively diagnose a UTI.
A negative nitrite result does not exclude a UTI.
A negative urine ketone result does not reliably exclude diabetic ketoacidosis.
Dipstick protein testing is not a substitute for quantitative urine albumin or protein measurement when indicated.
A urine dipstick cannot replace microscopy, culture or blood tests when these are clinically necessary.

rows: Supports the strip and allows handling
Contain chemicals that react with specific urine constituents
Provides the reference for interpreting colour changes
Protect unused strips from moisture, light and contamination
Identify the product, parameters, storage requirements and expiry date
Measures pad colour at specified wavelengths and standardises interpretation

content_groups.group_title: Common reagent pads and what they detect

rows: Suggests white blood cells in urine
Detects the peroxidase-like activity associated with haemoglobin or myoglobin
Detects selected ketone bodies, predominantly acetoacetate

blocks.text: Not all strips contain all ten parameters. Always check the specific manufacturer's instructions.
Rapid: most results are available within minutes.
Inexpensive: suitable for primary care, emergency departments and resource-limited settings.
Simple: requires minimal equipment and can be performed at the bedside.
Multiple tests at once: several chemical parameters can be assessed using one strip.
Small sample volume: only a small amount of urine is required.
Useful for screening: helps identify patients who need further investigations.
Portable: suitable for clinics, wards and outpatient departments.
Can guide clinical decisions: when interpreted alongside symptoms, examination and other investigations.
Semi-quantitative: results are generally reported as negative, trace, 1+, 2+ or similar categories rather than precise concentrations.
False-positive results: contamination, medications and chemical interference can affect certain pads.
False-negative results: dilute urine, short bladder incubation time, vitamin C and other interferences can affect results, depending on the parameter and product.
Timing-dependent: reading too early or too late can produce incorrect interpretations.
Storage-sensitive: moisture, heat, light and expired strips can affect reagent performance.
Limited sensitivity for some substances: for example, common ketone pads primarily detect acetoacetate rather than beta-hydroxybutyrate.
Does not identify organisms: a dipstick cannot determine the causative organism or its antibiotic susceptibility.
Clinical context is essential: an abnormal result does not automatically establish a diagnosis.
Examiner tip: Always state that a urine dipstick is a screening tool. Abnormal findings must be interpreted in context and confirmed with appropriate investigations when necessary.
Urine reagent strips in their original container.
Manufacturer's colour chart or compatible analyser.
Clean, appropriately labelled urine specimen.
Timer or watch.
Gloves and other appropriate PPE.
Appropriate waste container.
Request form or documentation system, if required.
Confirm the patient's identity using the required identifiers.
Explain the procedure and obtain consent where appropriate.
Collect urine in a clean, suitable container.
A fresh midstream urine specimen is often preferred for routine urinalysis and suspected UTI.
Mix the specimen gently if appropriate.
Test promptly, following the laboratory's specimen-handling policy.
Check the expiry date.
Check that the container has been stored according to the manufacturer's instructions.
Ensure the reagent pads are dry and have not deteriorated.
Remove one strip without touching the reagent pads unnecessarily.
Close the container immediately to protect the remaining strips from moisture.
Follow the specified immersion and reading times for that product.
Wear gloves when handling urine. Avoid splashes and contamination, perform hand hygiene, and dispose of the used strip and other consumables appropriately.
Important: Do not test a specimen that has been improperly stored without considering how storage may affect the results. If the specimen is unsuitable, recollect it when clinically appropriate.

subsections.subsection_title: How to perform a urine dipstick test — step-by-step OSCE demonstration

content_groups.group_title: Step 1: Introduce yourself and explain the procedure

blocks.text: “I will perform a urine dipstick test to check for chemical abnormalities in your urine. The test is quick and does not cause pain.”
Confirm identity, explain the procedure and obtain consent where appropriate.
Collect the specimen, urine dipstick, colour chart or analyser, timer and PPE.
Check the strip's expiry date and confirm that it has been stored correctly.

content_groups.group_title: Step 3: Inspect and prepare the urine specimen

blocks.text: Check the label, specimen suitability and appearance. Mix gently if required by the testing protocol.
If a UTI is suspected, use an appropriately collected specimen and arrange urine culture when indicated.
Perform hand hygiene and apply appropriate gloves before handling the specimen.
Take a single strip from the container, avoiding unnecessary contact with the reagent pads. Close the container immediately.
Dip the reagent areas into the urine for the duration specified by the manufacturer, ensuring the pads are exposed to the specimen.
Remove the strip promptly. Do not leave it submerged unnecessarily.
Gently drain excess urine and hold the strip horizontally to prevent reagent chemicals from running between adjacent pads.
Follow the manufacturer's instructions for removing excess fluid; do not wipe the reagent pads.
Start timing immediately. Different pads may have different reading times.
Many strips are read at specified intervals over approximately 30–120 seconds, but the exact times depend on the product. Do not use one universal reading time for every brand.
Compare each pad with its corresponding colour chart at the specified time, under suitable lighting.
Alternatively, use the compatible analyser according to its instructions.
Document the result for every reported parameter, including negative, trace, 1+, 2+ or other manufacturer-defined categories.
Include the specimen details and relevant clinical context.
Look for patterns rather than interpreting each pad in isolation.
Examples:
Leukocyte esterase and nitrite positivity may support a UTI diagnosis in a compatible clinical setting.
Glucose and ketones may suggest diabetes-related metabolic disturbance.
Protein and blood may warrant further renal or urinary tract assessment.
Bilirubin positivity may indicate conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and require further investigation.
Dispose of the used strip and consumables appropriately, remove gloves, perform hand hygiene and communicate significant findings.
Check → Collect → Dip → Drain → Time → Compare → Record → Interpret.
Urine dipstick testing itself is non-invasive and has no meaningful direct medical contraindication in routine use.
However, specimen collection, contamination and misinterpretation can cause problems.

rows: May cause misleading results; collect an appropriate sample
Can produce false readings; follow the manufacturer's instructions
May alter chemical and cellular findings
Can result in unnecessary treatment or missed disease
Avoid contact with reagent chemicals and follow product safety guidance
A negative result does not exclude every relevant disease

blocks.text: False-positive blood: may occur with contamination, oxidising agents or other sources of interference.
False-negative blood: vitamin C and other interferences may affect certain strips.
False-positive protein: alkaline urine and contamination can affect some protein reagent methods.
False-negative nitrite: can occur when urine has not remained in the bladder long enough, when dietary nitrate is low, or when the organism does not reduce nitrate.
False-negative ketones: standard nitroprusside-based tests may underestimate ketosis when beta-hydroxybutyrate predominates, as can occur in diabetic ketoacidosis.
Always consult the specific product instructions because interference varies between manufacturers.
A generally reassuring dipstick in an appropriate clinical context may show:

columns: Typical result in a healthy adult
rows: Negative or trace, depending on the method and context

blocks.text: Reference ranges vary by product, laboratory and clinical context. Urine pH and specific gravity vary physiologically with diet, hydration and other factors.
Typical pattern:
Leukocyte esterase positive.
Nitrite positive in some infections.
Blood may also be present.
Interpretation: these findings support a UTI when symptoms are compatible, but they are not diagnostic on their own.

A negative nitrite result does not exclude infection. Urine culture is particularly important when indicated by the patient's clinical condition, pregnancy, recurrent infection, complicated infection or treatment failure.
Possible findings:
Trace or greater protein reaction.
Persistent protein positivity on repeat testing.
Interpretation: proteinuria may occur in kidney disease, transient illness, fever, strenuous exercise or other conditions.
Persistent or clinically significant proteinuria should be assessed using appropriate quantitative tests, such as a urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR) or protein-to-creatinine ratio (PCR).
In pregnancy, proteinuria must be interpreted alongside blood pressure, symptoms and other clinical findings.
Interpretation: glucose in urine may occur when blood glucose exceeds the renal threshold, but it can also occur with renal glycosuria or certain medications.
Confirm suspected diabetes using appropriate blood glucose or HbA1c testing. A negative urine glucose result does not exclude diabetes.
Possible causes include:
Fasting or prolonged poor intake.
Vomiting.
A ketogenic diet.
Pregnancy-related metabolic disturbance.
Diabetic ketoacidosis.

Interpretation: ketones require clinical context. If diabetic ketoacidosis is suspected, assess blood glucose, blood beta-hydroxybutyrate, electrolytes and acid-base status as appropriate. Do not exclude DKA solely because urine ketones are negative.

content_groups.group_title: F. Haematuria or positive blood reaction

blocks.text: Possible findings:
Positive blood pad.
Microscopic or visible haematuria, depending on the clinical context.

Interpretation: a positive blood pad can reflect intact red cells, free haemoglobin or myoglobin. Confirm and investigate appropriately, often with urine microscopy and other tests guided by the presentation.

Interpretation: a positive bilirubin pad suggests conjugated bilirubin in urine and may be associated with hepatobiliary disease or cholestasis. Confirm with appropriate liver and biliary investigations.
Higher values: may occur with concentrated urine, glycosuria or other solutes.
Lower values: may occur with dilute urine or impaired urinary concentrating ability.

Interpret specific gravity alongside fluid status, medications, renal function and other clinical findings. Dipstick specific gravity is an estimate, not a definitive assessment of renal concentrating function.

content_groups.group_title: How to report a urine dipstick

blocks.text: Use a concise, structured report:
State that the test was performed on the identified specimen.
Report each parameter and its result.
Highlight clinically significant abnormalities.
Provide a cautious interpretation.
Recommend confirmation or further investigation where indicated.
Example:

“Urine dipstick demonstrates positive leukocyte esterase and nitrite, with trace blood. In a patient with compatible urinary symptoms, this supports a possible urinary tract infection. I would correlate with the clinical presentation and arrange urine culture when indicated.”
Urine dipsticks are widely used in pediatrics to investigate suspected UTI, renal disease, diabetes and metabolic disturbances.
Obtain a specimen using an age-appropriate collection method.
A clean-catch specimen is preferable when feasible.

A urine collection bag may be useful for screening, but positive culture results from bag-collected urine are prone to contamination and generally require confirmation using an appropriate collection method.
Follow local protocols for catheterisation or suprapubic aspiration when a reliable culture specimen is needed.
Do not delay urgent assessment of an unwell infant while attempting repeated specimen collection.
Interpret the dipstick alongside age, symptoms, fever and clinical condition.
Leukocyte esterase may suggest pyuria.
Nitrite positivity supports bacterial UTI in a compatible setting.
Negative results reduce the likelihood of UTI in some settings but do not exclude it in every child.
Urine culture is important when indicated by age, illness severity, discordant results or the local pediatric guideline.
Important: A febrile young infant or an unwell child requires prompt clinical assessment regardless of the dipstick result.

content_groups.group_title: C. Suspected diabetes or diabetic ketoacidosis

blocks.text: A child with polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, vomiting, abdominal pain or altered consciousness needs urgent assessment.
Check blood glucose promptly.
Measure blood ketones where available.
Assess electrolytes and acid-base status when DKA is suspected.
Do not use urine dipstick results alone to diagnose or exclude DKA.

Protein and blood on dipstick may indicate renal or urinary pathology. Persistent abnormalities require appropriate confirmation and evaluation, including renal function and quantitative urine protein testing when indicated.
Use the correct specimen collection technique.
Label specimens accurately.
Avoid contamination from stool, skin products or collection bags.
Interpret findings using age-appropriate clinical reference ranges and protocols.
Consider hydration, fever and recent exercise when interpreting results.
Useful when evaluating possible UTI.
Consider hepatobiliary disease and glycosuria.
Consider fasting, poor intake or metabolic emergencies.
Screen for proteinuria.
Assess urine acidity or alkalinity.
Interpret alongside bilirubin and the clinical picture.
Add blood and specific gravity to complete the commonly tested ten-parameter panel.

I — Interpret in context.
LE: Leukocyte esterase suggests white blood cells.
NIT: Nitrite may suggest nitrate-reducing bacteria.
Both positive results increase suspicion in a compatible clinical context, but neither alone proves a UTI.

subsections.subsection_title: Common OSCE questions and model answers

blocks.text: Q1. What is a urine dipstick?
Answer: A reagent strip used for rapid, semi-quantitative assessment of selected chemical constituents in urine.
Q2. What are the ten common parameters?
Answer: Leukocyte esterase, nitrite, blood, protein, glucose, ketones, pH, specific gravity, bilirubin and urobilinogen.
Q3. What is the significance of leukocyte esterase?
Answer: It suggests the presence of white blood cells in urine and may support a diagnosis of UTI when interpreted with symptoms and other findings.
Q4. Why can nitrite be negative in a patient with UTI?
Answer: The organism may not reduce nitrate, bladder incubation time may be insufficient, or dietary nitrate may be low. Other factors can also affect the result.
Q5. Does a positive protein dipstick diagnose nephrotic syndrome?

Answer: No. It suggests proteinuria, which requires clinical assessment and appropriate quantitative testing. Nephrotic syndrome requires assessment of the degree of protein loss and associated clinical and laboratory findings.
Q6. Can a urine dipstick exclude diabetes mellitus?
Answer: No. Urinary glucose can be absent despite diabetes. Use blood glucose or HbA1c testing as appropriate.
Q7. What is the major limitation of a urine ketone dipstick in DKA?
Answer: Most standard urine ketone strips detect acetoacetate rather than beta-hydroxybutyrate, which may predominate in DKA. Blood ketone measurement is preferred when available.
Q8. Why must the strip be read at the correct time?
Answer: Reagent colours develop over specified periods. Reading too early or too late can produce inaccurate results.
Q9. Why should the strip be held horizontally after dipping?
Answer: To reduce urine runoff between reagent pads, which can contaminate adjacent reactions and alter interpretation.
Q10. When is urine culture needed?

Answer: When indicated by the clinical presentation, including selected cases of suspected complicated or recurrent UTI, pregnancy, serious illness, treatment failure or pediatric infection according to local guidance.
Q11. What does a positive blood pad mean?
Answer: It detects haemoglobin-related peroxidase activity and may reflect red blood cells, free haemoglobin or myoglobin. Further assessment is guided by the clinical context.
Q12. What are the most important precautions?
Answer: Check expiry and storage, use a suitable specimen, follow manufacturer-specific immersion and reading times, avoid contamination and interpret results in context.

items: Mistake: Leaving the strip in the urine for too long

blocks.text: Dip it for the duration specified by the manufacturer and remove it promptly.

items: Mistake: Reading all pads at one arbitrary time

blocks.text: Different pads may require different reading intervals. Follow the product-specific instructions.

items: Mistake: Allowing urine to run between pads

blocks.text: Drain excess fluid as instructed and hold the strip horizontally.

items: Mistake: Leaving the reagent container open

blocks.text: Moisture can damage the strips. Close the container immediately after removing a strip.

items: Mistake: Diagnosing a UTI from the dipstick alone

blocks.text: Interpret the findings alongside symptoms, examination and culture when indicated.

items: Examiner tip: State the limitations clearly

blocks.text: A strong candidate explains false-positive and false-negative results and knows when confirmatory tests are necessary.
1. A patient has dysuria and urinary frequency. The dipstick shows positive leukocyte esterase but negative nitrite. What is the best interpretation?

items: UTI remains possible; interpret clinically and obtain culture when indicated
The patient definitely has renal failure

blocks.text: 2. Why are standard urine ketone strips potentially misleading in DKA?

items: They primarily detect acetoacetate and may underestimate beta-hydroxybutyrate

blocks.text: 3. What is the correct technique after removing the dipstick from urine?

items: Hold it vertically so urine runs between pads
Hold it horizontally after removing excess urine according to instructions

blocks.text: 4. A pregnant patient has protein on urine dipstick and elevated blood pressure. What is the appropriate response?

items: Diagnose pre-eclampsia from the dipstick alone
Ignore the result if the patient feels well

blocks.text: Urgently assess for a hypertensive disorder of pregnancy and arrange appropriate investigations

rows: Leukocytes, nitrite, blood, protein, glucose, ketones, pH, specific gravity, bilirubin and urobilinogen
Interpret leukocyte esterase and nitrite with symptoms
Confirm persistent or significant findings quantitatively
Check blood glucose and blood ketones; assess acid-base status as indicated
Follow the correct immersion and reading times
Record all parameters and interpret them in clinical context

blocks.text: Key principle: A urine dipstick is a screening test, not a definitive diagnosis. Correct technique, accurate timing and appropriate interpretation are essential.
